checks: Original candidate 8b5860c585f8735a at its pinned digest, §1, (1)–(2) and its proof, contains this claim. Covering the positive interior is sufficient: the family is finite and closed, so its union also covers the closure, and the depth maximizer used in the proof lies in the positive interior.

For A_i>α>0, the continuous distal mass function starts at A_i at b_i and tends to zero, so A_i−α is attained at a finite t_i>b_i. The full original band between b_i and t_i has mass α, since the hyperplanes are null. Intersection with the other retained sides can only reduce that band mass. Untrimmed caps already have mass at most α.

The mass V′ of the restriction is at least α/γ_r>0, so its convex positive interior is full dimensional. Changing boundary values on a null set and taking the inverse power on this open convex interior gives the extended convex inverse power for every β>r+1. At its attained deepest point a containing cap from the cover has mass at most α, so γ_r ≤ D(f′) ≤ α/V′ ≤ γ_r.

The equalities give that the union of the removed tails has mass equal to the sum of their masses. The excess multiplicity Σ_i 1_{tail i} − 1_{union} is nonnegative and at least one on each pairwise intersection. Its zero integral implies each intersection is f-null.

For every unit ray u, the change of radius s=ρ_T(u)t contributes ρ_T(u)^r times a single positive finite radial integral, so all through-y halfspaces have the corresponding fractions on uniform T. Any original halfspace containing y has f′-mass at least α. If its boundary missed y, the parallel shift through y would remove a positive-volume subset of an interior ball with positive f′-mass, contradicting the same lower bound for the shifted cap. A cap through y at equality has the oriented simplex vertex normal by 03bc771bddd39a8a.

Caps missing y avoid a common neighborhood, since there are finitely many closed caps. If the vertex j halfspace is absent, then on y+ε(v_j−y) each other barycentric coordinate drops from 1/(r+1) to (1−ε)/(r+1), so for sufficiently small ε>0 this point in U avoids every cap. This proves that all r+1 distinct types occur and exhaust the original caps.

In a positively trimmed tail, choose x in U strictly past the selected plane and strictly below all other retained thresholds. Pairwise f-null overlaps and null planes guarantee that choice. At y all retained thresholds have positive slack. The selected crossing on the segment is in the open convex U and strictly satisfies all the other retained inequalities. Moving slightly toward the retained side shows that a relatively open (r−1)-dimensional patch lies in the closure of the positive support of f′ on the selected supporting plane.

For R=∞ this support closure is the entire ambient space and cannot satisfy a retained upper bound. For R<∞ it is y+RT, and the canonical cap normal maximizes its affine barycentric coordinate only at the corresponding vertex. Since r≥2, a relative hyperplane patch cannot be contained in that vertex. Thus no positive trim occurs.

Conversely the canonical caps cover the whole space since the affine barycentric coordinates sum to one. A canonical cap of the uniform simplex is a homothety of factor r/(r+1) about its vertex, so the angular identity makes every cap fraction γ_r for f as well; substitution at α=γ_r V yields equality.
